question: In 2021, I already drew the Commission’s attention to the strategic risks of the acquisition of European Notified Bodies (NoBOs) by companies from third countries, due to their access to sensitive technical information and their crucial role in CE marking1.

The Commission emphasised that Member States are responsible for screening foreign investments and ensuring independent and proper supervision of quality standards2. However, Member States have indicated that this is the responsibility of the Commission. As a result, there are currently no structural screening or reporting obligations with regard to acquisitions of NoBOs.

The recent incident at DCI – a Dutch NoBo that abruptly ceased operations after being taken over by the Chinese NOA Group – reported on by the investigative journalism platform Follow the Money3, illustrates how very real these risks are: sensitive company files have disappeared, companies are being harmed and there are fears that information has found its way to China.
This is precisely the scenario which I warned about back in 2021. 1.
Does the Commission recognise the risks inherent in third-country parties acquiring NoBOs?

Is the Commission prepared to take measures – including carrying out an EU-wide investigation – to prevent such acquisitions and risky constructions in the future, in line with the European Parliament’s call to that effect4?

Answer to written question E-001186/2021(ASW), https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/E-92021-001186-ASW_EN.html “Chinese eigenaar doekt ineens Fries bedrijf op. Waar zijn de bedrijfsgeheimen van klanten?”, Follow the Money, 17 november 2025 (https://www.ftm.nl/artikelen/chinese-eigenaar-friese-keuringsclub-metnoorderzon-vertrokken). Report A9-0214/2022, paragraph 57.
answer: Regulation (EU) 2019/452 (1) establishes a framework for the screening of foreign direct investments (FDI) into the EU. In cases when an investment threatens the security or public order of more than one Member State, or when it could undermine a strategic project or programme of interest to the whole EU, the Commission can issue non-binding opinions.

Ultimately, however, it is for the national screening authorities of Member States to decide whether to authorise any given investment and under what conditions. Note that any information exchanged in the context of this regulation is to be treated as confidential and cannot by disclosed by the Commission.

On 11 December 2025, the co-legislators reached a provisional political agreement on the revision of the FDI screening regulation. The updated framework reinforces the EU’s ability to identify, assess and address risks posed by certain foreign investments, while preserving the EU’s openness to global trade and investment.
The revised framework will strengthen the current system by, among others, introducing a common minimum scope, mandatory screening obligations and covering intra-EU transactions.

Finally, the Joint Communication on strengthening EU economic security (2) refers to further actions by the Commission, including exploring a monitoring mechanism to identify startups in critical technology areas that are vulnerable to the risk of hostile foreign acquisitions.
